sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.

Introduction Research requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations. Developing such hypotheses involves gathering evidence, revising explanations, and deciding which directions merit further effort. This process generates experience about both the hypotheses under investigation and the decisions that guide their development, which allows human scientists to better design their next study. For research agents, using this experience to improve future research requires identifying useful contributions and translating them into changes to the model and research workflow. This motivates our central research question: How can research agents turn hypothesis development and investigation into recursive learning process that improves subsequent research? Addressing this question requires connecting hypothesis development and experimental execution with learning that improves the agent over investigations. Co-Scientist [8] develops hypotheses through multi-agent evolutionary refinement, while AI Scientist-v2 [33] connects hypothesis generation with experimental execution through agentic tree search. ScienceIDE [7] constructs learning environments from scientific codebases, and ScienceBuddy [32] turns researcher interactions into executable tasks and feedback for model and harness improvement. Building on these approaches, we focus on learning from hypotheses that agents actively develop: preserving how proposals evolve, link2 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses Figure 2 DiscoveryRSI couples multi-agent hypothesis development with recursive self-improvement. (a) Within an episode, Lead coordinates Generation and Evolution; candidate hypothesis versions are critiqued and progress is recorded. Selected hypotheses are compiled into Harbor tasks, with linked evidence, data, drafts, artifacts, assessments, contributions, and execution records. (b) Research trees carry hypotheses across RSI rounds: the recorded state 𝐻𝑘 enters RSI, which produces updated parameters (𝜃𝑘+1, 𝜓𝑘+1) and fresh questions for rediscovery. (c) Two update branches learn from the same experience: hypothesis credit optimization turns assessments and documented contributions into bounded weighted training, while harness replay keeps the model fixed, diagnoses recurring failures, and tests targeted workflow edits. Accepted updates are checked on the development set before round 𝑘 + 1. 3 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses ing assessments of research quality to the contributions behind them, and using this experience to improve subsequent investigations. Turning hypothesis development into recursive learning process presents challenges in both execution and learning. Translating proposal into an executable investigation requires resolving its data requirements and verification criteria while preserving the research question. Learning from the resulting research experience involves further challenge: hypothesiss final assessment does not specify which contributions should be reinforced. One agent may propose an explanation, another introduce useful control, and third revise the investigation plan in response to new evidence. Their contributions can remain obscured if only the final proposal is retained. Addressing these challenges involves making investigation plans concrete while preserving the development histories that connect assessments to the actions behind them. To address these challenges, we introduce DiscoveryRSI, general framework that turns hypothesis-driven research into recursive learning process (Figure 2). It develops research trees of testable hypotheses through multi-agent evolutionary search, preserving the evidence and decisions behind each proposal and revision. Selected computational investigations are compiled into executable Harbor tasks with concrete inputs, environments, required outputs, and verification checks. The retained research histories support three coupled recursive improvement mechanisms. Hypothesis credit optimization links assessments of research quality to documented contributions and assigns bounded credit to the contributing histories, providing supervision for the associated model actions. We use this supervision to train DiscoveryRSI-27B. Harness replay examines these histories to identify productive strategies and recurring failures, informing changes to agent coordination, evidence access, and research allocation. Rediscovery applies accepted model and harness updates to fresh investigations, generating new hypotheses and experience for subsequent learning. We introduce DFM-Bench to evaluate hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress. It assesses whether proposals are worthwhile and testable, what revisions contribute, and how development paths and research runs accumulate evidence and explore different directions. These assessments use hypotheses and their supporting research records, with the execution readiness of compiled Harbor tasks measured separately. Our contributions are fourfold: An operational definition and general framework for hypothesis-driven research. We define valuable and testable research hypotheses as joint objects comprising claim, an investigation plan, decision criteria, and alternative explanations (Definition 1). DiscoveryRSI develops these objects through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and preserves the underlying research decisions and development histories as reusable learning experience. Recursive self-improvement from research experience. We develop hypothesis credit optimization to attribute assessments of research quality to documented contributions and train DiscoveryRSI-27B, harness replay to refine research strategies and workflows, and rediscovery to apply accepted improvements to subsequent investigations. 4 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses benchmark for hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress. DFMBench evaluates hypotheses, revisions, development paths, research runs, and research contributions. We further evaluate DiscoveryRSI through expert-supervised review and controlled model comparisons with its base model and other research agents. Results show clear gains over rounds of self-improvements and changes in agent behavior patterns. Empirical evidence for learning from scientific research. DiscoveryRSI increase mean hypothesis quality from 4.86 to 5.39, with gains in falsifiability, alternative explanations, and data resolvability. Expert-supervised assessment shows greater human-rated improvement along research paths, with an average gain per revision of +0.07, compared with +0.03 for GPT-5.6 Sol and 0.01 for GPT-6 Luna. DiscoveryRSI-27B also achieves 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with post-cutoff research, compared with 2.5% for GPT-6 and 2.3% for Claude Opus 5. Together, these findings show that learning from research histories improves the formulation of testable investigations and the development of hypotheses toward concrete research opportunities. 2. Valuable and Testable Research Hypotheses 2.1. An Operational Definition We introduce joint operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses for hypothesis-driven research agents. It makes the scientific value of claim and the evidential capacity of its investigation explicit within one revisable research object. Definition 1 (Valuable and testable research hypothesis) Relative to documented evidence base and declared data, experimental, and resource constraints B, research hypothesis is represented as = (𝑐, 𝜋, 𝑑, 𝑎), where 𝑐 is an evidence-grounded claim, 𝜋 an investigation plan, 𝑑 its decision criteria, and 𝑎 the relevant alternative explanations. It is valuable when resolving the uncertainty in 𝑐 could make consequential addition to current understanding or change justified research decision relative to E. It is testable when 𝜋 specifies an investigation feasible under whose observable outcomes, interpreted through 𝑑 and 𝑎, can provide evidence that supports, weakens, or bounds 𝑐, with unresolved distinctions stated explicitly. valuable and testable research hypothesis satisfies both requirements. (1) The four components make this definition operational. The claim specifies the system or population, scope, observable quantities, and scientific uncertainty. The investigation plan identifies the data or measurements, comparisons, controls, analysis, and required dependencies. The decision criteria state, before interpreting results, which outcomes would support or weaken the claim and which would remain inconclusive. The alternative explanations identify competing accounts, confounding, or measurement limitations, together with the comparisons that can distinguish them and the limits of those comparisons. Scientific value can arise from new explanation, useful replication, measurement check, or an informative negative result when it changes understanding or research priorities. Testability depends on the declared evidence and constraints: unavailable measurements or experiments remain explicit dependencies until they can be obtained. 5 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses These requirements assess proposed research opportunity; they do not establish that the claim is true. DFM-Bench evaluates the resulting objects through its scientific-quality profile (Section 4), while completed execution and independent support are recorded separately. 2.2. From Observations to Research Questions DiscoveryRSI focuses on how research question is formed and tied to available evidence. IdeaScientist develops proposals from specified problem and challenge, including evaluation plans and falsifiable predictions [19]. Our emphasis is the joint development of hypothesis and the investigation that can examine it: observations and data constraints shape the question, its comparisons, alternative explanations, and interpretation. Descriptive analyses characterize observed patterns, variation, and measurement coverage, helping identify questions worth pursuing and the evidence available to investigate them. Each proposal then ties its claim to defined system or population, observable quantities, and interpretable outcomes. 2.3. Hypothesis with an Investigation Plan Figure 3 instantiates Definition 1 with MIMIC-IV proposal. Its value lies in asking whether repeated creatinineurine output mismatch adds information about adverse outcomes after ICU discharge. Its testability comes from defined population and outcome window, patient-level held-out comparisons against simpler baselines, explicit interpretation criteria, and alternative explanations that bound the claim. supported lack of added information would also inform whether more complex models merit further investigation. Recorded hypothesis versions retain links to their predecessors and supporting evidence. These records make changes in the question, investigation plan, and interpretation traceable, providing the research histories used by the trees and learning mechanisms in the following section. 3. DiscoveryRSI DiscoveryRSI develops research hypotheses across episodes and retains the work behind each version as linked research records (Figure 2). These records connect scientific assessments to contributing actions for model training, and connect execution failures to changes in the research harness. Selected investigations become executable Harbor tasks. Hypothesis credit optimization, harness replay, and rediscovery then turn this accumulated experience into recursive learning process. DFM-Bench: Evaluating Scientific Quality and Research Progress DFM-Bench evaluates scientific inquiry through five connected questions: whether hypothesis is worthwhile and testable, what revision contributes, whether development path accumulates useful evidence, how research run allocates effort, and what distinct scientific contribution emerges. Each question requires evidence appropriate to its level. Table 1 Evaluation coverage of selected scientific-discovery benchmarks. check denotes explicit assessment, circle related or partial assessment, and cross no explicit assessment under our definitions. Recording intermediate actions alone does not establish coverage. Definitions and qualifications appear in Appendix D.6. Scientific assessment Research-process assessment Benchmark Hypothesis Contribution Evidence use Revision Development Whole-run merit maturity path allocation AgentIdeaBench [22] DiscoveryBench [21] BLADE [9] ScienceAgentBench [3] OEB [28] DFM-Bench (ours) 4.1. Five Levels of Scientific Assessment Hypothesis quality. Is an individual hypothesis worthwhile and testable? Assessment examines the proposal, investigation plan, and supporting evidence. It produces 10 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses scientific-quality profile covering importance, novelty, grounding, falsifiability, data resolvability, feasibility, alternative explanations, and actionability, together with an aggregate score when the required assessments are complete. Revision value. What did revision contribute? Assessment compares hypothesis with its actual predecessor and examines the evidence and actions supporting the change. It distinguishes substantive progress, necessary repair, repetition, and insufficient evidence. Changes in hypothesis scores are recorded separately from these judgments. Development-path progress. Does development path accumulate useful evidence? Assessment follows an ordered sequence of actual ancestry relationships, examining evidence acquisition, coherent revision, scientific continuity, and decisions to continue or stop. Agent action histories provide supporting evidence for these judgments, while the development path records how the hypotheses themselves changed. Research-run quality. Does research run explore and allocate effort productively? Assessment examines the full research graph, selection and stopping decisions, and available opportunity and resource records. It considers the breadth and depth of exploration, synthesis across branches, and allocation of the research budget. Run-level quality is assessed directly rather than obtained by averaging path scores. Scientific contribution. What distinct scientific contribution emerges across related proposals? Assessment groups proposals by scientific question and records what was added beyond the starting evidence: new distinction, an informative negative result, supported finding, or reduction in uncertainty. Contribution maturity distinguishes proposed ideas from contributions supported by completed investigations and independent checks. 4.2. Coverage Relative to Existing Benchmarks Existing benchmarks examine complementary aspects of scientific work, including ideation, goal-directed discovery, analytical decisions, and executable tasks [3, 9, 21, 22]. OEB further evaluates evidence use, experimentation, and research-process integrity [28]. DFM-Bench makes hypotheses, revisions, development paths, research runs, and contribution families explicit assessment objects. Table 1 compares their evaluation coverage; the accompanying definitions and qualifications appear in Appendix D.6. 5. Expert-Supervised Assessment of Scientific Hypotheses We conduct expert-supervised human assessment to examine the scientific value and design quality of generated hypotheses. The review considers whether proposed investigation addresses worthwhile question, fits the available data, distinguishes alternative explanations, and yields interpretable outcomes. The assessment involved 27 medical doctors, medical students and bioscience PhD students with prior biomedical or clinical research backgrounds, under three senior supervisors. The review cohort contains 292 proposals from six dataset groups spanning the four life-science domains: HCC clinical cohort (52), MIMIC-IV (60), eICU (60), UK Biobank (55), GEO targets (35), and GEO mechanisms (30). Proposals were drawn from fixed hypothesis-atlas snapshot and presented in randomized order. 11 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses Anonymous proposal packets. Reviewers received English proposal copies containing the scientific question, investigation plan, data requirements, alternative explanations, and supporting citations. Producer and execution provenance were withheld, while scientific methods and references were retained. AI reviewer grades were hidden, and reviewers were instructed to assess each proposal on its own merits without consulting its revision history in the atlas. The interface presented the proposal alongside the assessment form (Figure 4); Appendix consolidates the review protocol. Scientific judgments and design flaws. The protocol asks reviewers to record an overall research-value judgment first, using five-point scale from not worth pursuing to top priority, together with recommendation to prioritize, revise, defer, or reject the proposal. Reviewers then assess six criteria on anchored four-point scales: importance, advance over known work, plausible and evidence-bounded claims, data fit, alternative explanations, and informative results. separate verdict identifies whether consequential design flaw is absent, fixable, or fatal. Cant judge is available when evidence or relevant expertise is insufficient. flaw checklist, description of the main flaw, and further comments are optional. (b) Reviewers record an overall judgment, assess six anchored criteria, and identify design flaws; flaw details and comments are optional. The criterion list summarizes the rubric, while radio-option excerpts reproduce one saved assessment. Identifying metadata is omitted. The example illustrates the review procedure rather than an aggregate evaluation result. 6. Experimental Setup Research domains. We evaluate DiscoveryRSI across four life-science domains: clinical and population health, therapeutic target prioritization, disease mechanisms, and population multi-omics. Inputs include the HCC clinical cohort, MIMIC-IV [13], eICU [25], UK Biobank [31], and molecular studies from GEO and ArrayExpress [6, 27]. 12 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses Agents inspect data and literature, formulate hypotheses, and develop investigation plans specifying comparisons, measurements, and interpretation criteria (Figure 5). Battery setting. To test transfer beyond life science, we add battery setting with four domains: electrical diagnostics, health prediction, degradation mechanisms, and usage history and aging. The evidence pack covers capacity and impedance aging measurements [20], impedance-based health prediction [14, 42], degradation-mode analysis [15, 17], and path-dependent aging experiments [26]. Investigations separate measured quantities from fitted degradation labels and specify cell, condition, and protocol splits. The same LeadGenerationEvolutionCritiqueCompiler loop is used, with battery-specific checks for operating conditions, sensing, physical plausibility, and competing explanations. Hypothesis-credit training. We perform full-parameter fine-tuning of DiscoveryRSI-27B with 256K-token context window using hypothesis-credit-weighted supervision. From 15,792 collected research trajectories, attribution, filtering, and tokenization yield 2,397 training trajectories: 634 Lead, 861 Generation, and 902 Evolution histories. The training sequences contain 291.12 million tokens, of which 6.18 million (2.12%) receive direct supervision. We train for one epoch using Adam with learning rate of 5 106, global batch size of 16, and BF16 precision. Detailed trajectory accounting, credit allocation, and token masking appear in Appendix C. Evaluation. We examine four questions: whether hypothesis quality improves across research rounds, how research behavior changes, whether human reviewers recognize useful revisions, and whether hypotheses inspire subsequent research. Automated quality evaluation covers 241 research questions across the four domains using GPT-5.6 Sol as the judge. Behavioral analysis examines six campaigns of 20 episodes per evaluated model variant. Human assessment covers 292 proposals reviewed by 27 participants with biomedical or clinical research backgrounds under three senior supervisors. Proposals are presented in randomized order with model identities and automated scores hidden (Section 5). Literature-based evaluation uses shared reference corpus with modelspecific temporal cutoffs. 7. Results Battery-domain DFM. The battery applies the five-level DFM-Bench evaluation to 200 episodes and 351 generated hypotheses, with three AI reviews per hypothesis. The current panel reports mean hypothesis quality of 5.61 on 165 complete scores, substantive progress on 214 of 366 transitions (58.47%), mean complete-trajectory score of 81.52 across 152 paths, and research round score of 71.25. 20 contribution families were identified, with 7 carrying diagnostic or research evidence. 7.1. RQ1: Does learning from research histories improve hypothesis quality? Hypothesis quality rises with each round of self-improvement. Mean automated hypothesis quality increases from 4.86 for the base model to 5.18 after the first research round and 5.39 after the second (Figure 6). The second-round model exceeds the base model in all four domains, with gains ranging from 0.28 points in disease mechanisms to 0.94 points in population multi-omics. The additional gain decreases from 0.32 in the first round to 0.21 in the second. DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses Figure 5 Shared research process across life-science and battery domains. The process strip summarizes how evidence becomes question, investigation, and evidence-bounded interpretation with iterative critique. The two rows show the four life-science domains and four battery domains used in the experiments. Improvements concentrate on the specification of testable investigations. Falsifiability rises from 4.00 to 6.20, consideration of alternative explanations from 4.44 to 5.98, data resolvability from 3.73 to 4.99, and feasibility from 4.79 to 5.87. These changes indicate more explicit tests, better-defined evidence requirements, and clearer interpretation of possible outcomes. Gains are uneven: importance declines from 6.48 to 6.04 and novelty from 4.87 to 4.58. The observed improvement therefore concerns investigation design more strongly than the perceived significance or originality of research questions. 7.2. RQ2: How does DiscoveryRSI change research behavior? DiscoveryRSI allocates more effort to developing existing hypotheses. Evolve and repair operations increase from 77.5% of episodes for the base model to 90.0% after the first round and 91.7% after the second. Restarts decrease from 21.7% to 5.8% and 5.0%, respectively (Figure 7). The shift is especially pronounced in episodes 1120, where restarts fall from approximately 32% for the base model to 3% after the second round. Hypothesis development paths become more evidence-driven. Development-path scores increase most for evidential and inferential discipline (+1.25), followed by technical and knowledge exploration (+0.34) and scientific continuity and synthesis (+0.24). Changes in cumulative progress, stopping decisions, and budget efficiency remain below 0.1 points, while disciplinary connections decline by 0.28. Together, these results suggest more sustained refinement and stronger evidential discipline, with limited improve14 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses Figure 6 Automated hypothesis quality across self-improvement rounds. (a) Top: example research tree from each round; color shows weighted quality across eight evaluation axes. Middle: mean hypothesis quality per round. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals and shading shows the interquartile range. Bottom: mean quality per domain with 95% confidence intervals. (b) Mean and axis-specific scores. All scores are produced by the automated grader using the weights in Appendix D. Figure 7 Changes in research behavior across rounds. (a) Share of each action across all episodes in round. (b) Share of campaigns taking each action at each episode position, sampled from six campaigns per round; blank cells indicate 0%. (c) Change in development-path scores from the base model to round 2. 15 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses ment in broader exploration or resource allocation. Operation frequencies describe the research strategy; their value depends on the quality of the resulting revisions. 7.3. RQ3: Do human reviewers recognize improvements in the hypotheses? Human assessment identifies favorable balance of revision outcomes for DiscoveryRSI27B. Within the assessed research trees, 41% of revisions improve the mean human score, 47% leave it unchanged, and 12% reduce it. The corresponding proportions are 31%, 37%, and 32% for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 25%, 44%, and 31% for GPT-6 Luna. Mean score change per revision is +0.07 for DiscoveryRSI-27B, compared with +0.03 and 0.01 for the two comparison models (Figure 8). These results measure progress within research trees and provide complementary evidence to the comparisons across research rounds. Figure 8 Human assessment of hypothesis quality and revision progress. (a) Mean ratings across six criteria on 14 scale. (b) Mean score change per revision. (c) Fractions of improved, unchanged, and worse revisions, in the same model order as panel (b). Absolute quality ratings show mixed profile. DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on importance (3.10 versus 2.94) and plausible, evidence-bounded claims (3.37 versus 3.16). Both receive 2.31 for advance over known work, while GPT-6 Luna scores higher on data fit, alternative explanations, and informative results. Out of all the proposals, Thus, the stronger revision outcomes coexist with remaining weaknesses in individual proposals. revision path in MIMIC-IV. MIMIC-IV development path illustrates how useful revisions improve an investigation (Figure 9). Successive versions clarify the time origin and 48-hour landmark, bind variables to available data fields, and specify acute kidney injury thresholds. The mean of six human-rated criteria increases from 2.83 to 3.50; data fit and informative results each improve by two points. This example connects revision gains to concrete design changes. Other branches retain consequential flaws, including 16 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses two depth-four siblings with unspecified acute kidney injury thresholds, underscoring the need to evaluate each resulting proposal. Figure 9 Design changes and human ratings along revision path. (a) MIMIC-IV path and assessed siblings; node values are six-criterion means on 14 scale. Numbered changes are explained below the tree. Dashed ochre nodes mark fatal flaws; the two final fatal siblings lack specified AKI thresholds. (b) Criterion ratings along the highlighted path. 7.4. RQ4: Do the hypotheses inspire subsequent research? We define inspiration as concrete connection between generated hypothesis and subsequent literature. publication after the recorded cutoff must provide an experimental design, comparator, measurement, or testable evidence gap relevant to developing or testing the hypothesis. Across the two pooled DiscoveryRSI production runs, 74 of 1,176 hypothesis versions meet this criterion, giving an inspiration rate of 6.3%. The corresponding rates are 5.4% for DeepSeek (14/257), 2.8% for GLM (1/36), 2.5% for GPT (59/2,341), and 2.3% for Claude (3/131). DiscoveryRSI reaches 16.9% in therapeutic targets, 7.4% in population multi-omics, 6.8% in disease mechanisms, and 2.3% in clinical and population health (Figure 10). These descriptive results indicate that DiscoveryRSI hypotheses more frequently connect to concrete research directions in the retrieved literature. Group sizes, domain composition, temporal cutoffs, and retrieval coverage differ, and multiple versions may belong to the same research family. Prospective tracking is needed to determine whether researchers adopt these hypotheses and pursue the proposed investigations. Literature comparison protocol. We construct shared reference corpus through 420 backward and forward citation traversals, yielding 17,790 citation edges and 16,440 resolved publications. References are filtered using each model groups recorded cutoff. Corpus construction, cutoff handling, retrieval, and auditing are detailed in Appendix F. Why does Claude Opus 5 have lower inspiration rate? We attribute part of Claude Opus 5s lower measured rate to retrieval coverage and proposal format. Only 15 of its 131 proposals pass the retrieval gate (11.5%), compared with 355 of 1,176 for DiscoveryRSI27B (30.2%). Among these retrieved proposals, however, the positive-judgment fractions are similar: 20.0% and 20.8%, respectively. Claudes median proposal length is 41,134 characters, while retrieval uses the first 6,000 characters and the semantic audit sees the first 2,500. Provenance and revision notes can therefore displace scientific content from the evaluated excerpt. In diagnostic using proposal titles as queries while retaining the corpus, scoring method, date rule, and overlap threshold, Claudes retrieval passage increases from 15 to 95 proposals. This sensitivity supports format-related retrieval explanation, but does not establish additional matches meeting the inspiration criterion. 8. Related Work Discovery agents and evaluation. Discovery agents increasingly support hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and computational investigation. Co-Scientist develops hypotheses through multi-agent refinement [8], AI Scientist-v2 connects research ideation with agentic experimental search [33], and Biomni integrates biomedical tools and data [12]. Discovery Foundation Models frame problem formation and evidence-grounded 18 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses revision as learnable capabilities [35], while ScienceIDE constructs environments for learning from scientific workflows [7]. Evaluation spans scientific ideation in AgentIdeaBench [22], data-driven discovery in DiscoveryBench and BLADE [9, 21], executable investigations in ScienceAgentBench [3], and research-process assessment in OEB [28]. DiscoveryRSI connects hypothesis development to subsequent model learning, while DFM-Bench makes hypotheses, revisions, development paths, research runs, and contribution families explicit evaluation objects. Learning from evaluated research experience. Reward-guided training provides foundation for converting generated experience into model updates. RAFT selects highly rated samples for fine-tuning [5], ReST-EM alternates generation and feedback-based filtering [30], and advantage-weighted regression learns through weighted likelihood objectives [24]. SimpleTES further studies learning from scientific exploration trajectories [37]. These approaches motivate the use of assessed research histories as supervision. DiscoveryRSI addresses the attribution problem within multi-agent hypothesis development: an assessment concerns scientific proposal, whereas learning targets belong to the histories that contributed to it. Hypothesis credit optimization links these levels through documented contributions, bounded credit allocation, and supervision restricted to supported assistant actions. Persistent and recursive agent improvement. Reflexion, GEPA, and ACE retain experience through verbal memory, prompt evolution, and contextual playbooks [1, 29, 41]; harness optimization extends adaptation to agent workflows and implementations [18, 38]. Darwin Gödel Machine and Hyperagents study persistent program-level improvement [39, 40], while MASS couples multi-agent workflow optimization with learning from selected executions [16]. ScienceBuddy connects harness refinement with model learning [32], and RSI-Anything uses predictive world models to guide interaction and retained system updates [4]. DiscoveryRSI brings these directions to hypothesis-centered research: evolving claims, evidence, and investigation decisions provide shared record for contribution-based model learning, harness replay, and subsequent rediscovery. Its focus is how experience accumulated while developing scientific questions can improve later investigations. 9. Conclusion DiscoveryRSI connects hypothesis development with learning from documented research contributions. The present work reaches concrete hypotheses and compiled investigation plans. The next step is to determine which proposals merit investigation, using solvers and frameworks such as RSI-Anything [4] to execute, assess, and refine them. Closing the discovery loop further requires wet-lab validation and methods that turn supportive, negative, and inconclusive outcomes into improved research decisions. Extending hypothesis discovery and DFM-Bench to additional scientific domains will help establish how these capabilities generalize. Together, these directions advance the DFM vision [35] of agents that formulate worthwhile questions, investigate them, and learn from the resulting evidence. 19 DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
